extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics; aspiring poets
extracted.subtask_description: A set of critical standards and aesthetic principles for judging poets and poetry (especially modern/living poets), drawn from a lecture on poetic genius, style, and the qualities that make ballads, lyric poems, and drama succeed or fail. Useful for critics, students, and practitioners assessing poetic worth and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring fame vs popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame is the recompense not of the living, but of the dead; it is not popularity, the shout of the multitude, the venal puff, or flattering favour, but 'the spirit of a man surviving himself in the minds and thoughts of other men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that can survive posterity; do not mistake immediate applause or fashion for true merit. Artists should be prepared to wait for the judgment of time rather than mortgage their reputation for transient praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of nature as the first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of nature is the first thing in the mind of the true poet; truth and nature are the source of poetic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should spring from an intimate and authentic relationship with nature and natural feeling rather than self-admiration or mere verbal display. Evaluate poets by their fidelity to natural truth and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and self-effacement in the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: He who would be great in the eyes of others must first learn to be nothing in his own; admiration of self should be last, the love of excellence first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid valuing poets for self-display or personal celebrity. A genuine poet focuses on subject and truth, not on self-promotion or vanity—evaluate motive and stance as part of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and simplicity over ornament and finery
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of poets like Rogers and Campbell: they 'wrap up obvious thoughts in a glittering cover of fine words,' substituting decoration for truth; such work lacks 'truth of nature or simplicity of expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity, simplicity, and truthful feeling to elaborate, ambiguous, or over-finished diction. Beware of 'tinsel words', strained epigrams, and verbal finery that obscure meaning rather than reveal it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological realism and diversity of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Miss Baillie's tragedies treat passions as 'one and indivisible' and reduce characters to moral puppets; this is a deficiency in dramatic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic characters should display complex, varied, and credible passions rather than acting as didactic mouthpieces. Evaluate plays for believable emotional complexity and internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness and logical fitness of imagery and antithesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell's lines contain 'curiosa infelicitas' where antithesis or imagery fails (example: 'Some hamlet shade, to yield his sickly form / Health in the breeze, and shelter in the storm'—the antithesis misfires because the breeze, not the shade, yields health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetic figures for logical coherence and aptness: metaphors, antitheses, and images must make sense and suit their contexts. Avoid forced or elegant turns of phrase that are logically or sensibly unsound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of feeling and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Works like The Cotter's Saturday Night and certain ballads exhibit 'noble and pathetic' pictures of human manners and a 'lofty devotional spirit'—they touch deeply because of genuine feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value authenticity of emotion and devotional or moral seriousness when present. Pathos should arise naturally from human interest and character, not from contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity to traditional/national forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Old Scotch ballads and early minstrel songs are praised for their original cast of thought, intimacy with nature, and national character; successful imitations capture that simplicity and native feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating songs, ballads, or imitations, consider their faithfulness to the traditional genre's tone, imagery, and simplicity. Imitations succeed when they preserve the original's spirit rather than polishing it away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in critical enthusiasm for living poets
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be certain which living poets will endure; therefore critics should 'husband our enthusiasm' and avoid premature extravagant praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution in awarding high praise to contemporaries; be mindful that haste or excessive enthusiasm can mislead readers and distort future judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness and avoidance of personal bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal acquaintance with living poets can create prejudice and impair free judgment; poets do not praise one another in hyperbole and friendship may distort critical views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should acknowledge potential biases arising from friendship or social intimacy and aim for impartial assessment; separate personal relations from aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of expression to subject (avoid meaningless refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poetical works sacrifice sense and keeping to 'a jingle of words'—a decomposition of prose into ornament without substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether style serves substance. Elegant phrasing must carry meaning; opposed to mere sound or fashionable diction that leaves little to express.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality and heartfelt song over mere technical display
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple, artless tunes of national lays (Dundee, Martyrs, Elgin) are 'the sweetest' and produce 'heart-felt raptures' unlike artificial Italian trills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In lyric and song, prefer natural musical feeling and heartfelt tone to technical vocal display. Assess whether the music/metrical choices genuinely move the reader/listener.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original, nature-grounded imagery and romantic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The best ballad-style love-songs show romantic imagery intimately tied to nature (thistle's glittering down, gilliflower, horseman's silver bells, the hawk on its perch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value imagery that feels rooted in concrete natural detail and original observation rather than clichéd ornament. Look for sensory, specific images that convey feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize genre-appropriate strengths (genre fitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Female writers praised as novelists (Mrs. Inchbald, Mrs. Radcliffe, Madame D'Arblay) may excel in their genre without being 'poetical'; assess authors within the conventions and strengths of their chosen form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should account for genre conventions and the particular aims of a work; do not judge a novelist solely by poetic standards, or vice versa—evaluate fitness to purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of interest and precision of dramatic outline
rubrics_metrics.description: De Montfort (Miss Baillie) is praised for 'a nerve, a continued unity of interest, a setness of purpose and precision of outline'—qualities that suit the stage and a strong leading actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In tragedy and serious drama, value sustained unity, coherent purpose, and carefully drawn character outlines. Assess dramatic works for structural coherence and focused intent.
